paragraphs: Three days after the battle on the Fei River, the banks still smelled of soaked leather armor and dead horses. Qin had first moved its wounded to the high ground. Each camp had to verify its list of dead anew, and prisoners were entered in a separate register. Fu Rong lay in the medical tent with his right leg splinted and his fever not yet gone. When he heard that younger generals were urging pursuit of Liu Yu, he had the military map carried to his bed. Propping himself halfway up, he wrote a note ordering the pursuit stopped. His hand shook so badly that several characters almost wandered off the paper.
“His Majesty has already given that order,” his attendant said.
“Send mine as well,” Fu Rong replied. “If they ask why, they’ll have another piece of paper to read.”

Fu Jian saw his brother’s crooked handwriting and ordered the note filed with the army’s orders. The opportunity for pursuit had passed, but the war was not over. Though Jin’s army had retreated, its fleets, Jingkou forces, and the garrisons around Jiankang remained. The road south was no straight highway from the Fei River to the gates of the Jin palace. Channels wound through the land, defenses on the Yangtze were unbroken, and behind the army lay the unresolved dispute over the three towns. To take Jiankang, they would first have to traverse great stretches of territory whose allegiance was still contested.

Qin spent half a month repairing usable pontoon crossings on the southern side and bringing up skiffs and large boats for the passage of the Yangtze. The first attempts went badly. A fortified settlement in Huainan offered transit but refused provisions. Its clan elder explained that he had once carried grain for Huan Xuan, and after Huan Xuan’s defeat the unpaid vouchers were still at the bottom of a chest. If he now accepted a Qin voucher, from whom would he collect the debt when rulers changed again? The Qin supply clerk left a grain-purchase certificate endorsed by central command, promising repayment through government granaries, rather than forcing the gates and taking food.

Several old ferry crossings upstream on the Yangtze were still held by Jin troops. Taking advantage of the current after rain, Qin marines captured a landing on a sandy islet, but Jin archery boats beat back the first soldiers ashore and destroyed four vessels. Fu Pi led the following ships into a narrower branch of the river, drawing the sentry boats away in daylight before landing troops under cover of the rising water at night.

The transports queued for three days at the shoals. Many northern soldiers had never seen the great river and found its black water stretching beyond sight, with the planks beneath them heaving more than the skiffs on the Fei. Some vomited until they could no longer stand; others clung to mooring posts. Their officers did not threaten them with cowardice charges and force them into the current. Naval regulations required them to practice rowing near shore first, then cross with their units.

The Qin vanguard that reached the south numbered only several tens of thousands. Its principal grain route remained on the northern bank, with supplies relayed in stages by the fleet. Southern Jin troops fell back from several old camps and did not again meet Qin with the strength assembled on the Fei; neither, however, did local gentry and fortified-estate owners offer submission. Some opened markets and sold rice, others shut their gates and loosed arrows. Liu Yu had withdrawn his Beifu elite. The remaining units blocked bridges when they could, then fell back into woodland. Every ten li the Qin advanced, they had to leave men guarding a landing or repairing a stretch of destroyed road. By the time Fu Jian reached the southern forward camp, winter rain had fallen for six days without pause.

He climbed a high ridge and saw Jiankang for the first time. Mount Zhong lay east of the city, its lower slopes hidden in rain and mist. The Qinhuai waterways ran through the walls; government residences and temples rose and fell beneath wet clouds. Merchant sails were fewer on the Yangtze, yet a handful of white sails had not been furled.

The veteran soldiers accompanying him knew the old city of Chang’an and the charred palace walls of Ye. At the sight of Jiankang’s endless rooftops they were struck speechless. Rumors passed quietly that every palace beam was fragrant sandalwood and that capturing the gates would let them divide the great families' treasures. By the time such stories traveled down the grain carts to the river mouth, men were already writing home that one southern copper vault held the wealth of several northern counties.

The letters were examined the next day. Central command did not forbid soldiers to write to their families. It singled out language promising plunder as reward and sent it to the squad officers, ordering them to explain the established rules for military merit and payment. A troop leader from Hedong argued that he had marched wounded all the way from Baishi; if men could not even dream of taking a good blanket, how would they survive the wet winter? The military magistrate did not scold him. He opened the compensation vouchers for men lost from the unit and said two more bereaved families had received grain only the previous night. If they robbed a household in Jiankang today, who would keep faith with those vouchers tomorrow?

The debate in the main tent was fiercer. Although Qin had won at the Fei River, many soldiers and generals had never approached the Jin capital before. They wanted to storm it before Liu Yu recovered and while the city’s defenses remained incomplete. One calculated that simultaneous attacks from the North Fence Gate to Stone City could bring tens of thousands of infantry to bear and open a breach within days. Another proposed taking the imperial palace first, then ordering the Three Wu commanderies to submit their registers.

It was easy for generals to move their hands across a map. The grain officer, however, presented a newly copied inventory of southern troops and provisions. Government granaries inside the city were separate from private stores held by the great clans. Jingkou’s fleet remained intact. Jingzhou still had garrisons that the Jin court could not fully control. If several river mouths were blocked overnight, the Qin vessels conducting the siege would be the first to run short of food.
Fu Jian asked, “If we assault from two points, what casualties should we expect?”

The siege engineer estimated several thousand Qin soldiers at least; once the army entered densely inhabited quarters, no one could calculate the dead and wounded. Another general said that was always the price of storming a city and that delay would only invite trouble. Fu Jian asked him to look at a different map. It showed no walls, only rivers and canals, neighborhoods, mulberry fields, and granaries. If southern troops concentrated around the palace, Qin soldiers would have to fight through ward after ward. Even if they seized the throne, the fleets and powerful families of Wu, Kuaiji, Jingkou, and Jingzhou would still be where they were. Jiankang would become a wasteland of ashes, while Qin’s army searched for food among southern waterways it did not know.

Fu Rong came into the tent on a crutch despite his illness. He was pale, and tested his weight gingerly every time his right foot touched the ground. An officer sprang up to support him, only to be waved away. Studying the city map, Fu Rong said that Liu Yu had abandoned neither banners nor boats in his retreat from the Fei. Now he had brought his elite back to Jiankang and was waiting for Qin to storm the walls. If Qin soldiers mistakenly killed even one household in the city, people who had refused Liu Yu grain yesterday would pick up knives and defend their gates for him tomorrow.
“Aren’t you afraid he’ll counterattack?” Fu Jian asked.
“I am,” Fu Rong said. “But if we charge now, we’ll raise his army for him all the sooner.”
A veteran general objected. “Then how long are we supposed to sit outside the walls?”

Fu Rong did not answer at once. With the tip of his staff he indicated the roads to the markets. “Keep military grain, weapons, and reinforcements from going in. Don’t shut off the people’s salt, rice, and medicines entirely. If you can’t tell the two apart, send someone who can. It takes men, boats, and patience to do that—more trouble than pushing a few siege ladders.”

Fu Jian had the assault plan moved to a side table and summoned army command, the finance office, and the officials responsible for the southern ferries to determine the lines of containment together. The first line would seal military roads against large shipments of weapons and reinforcements. The second would guard ferries and markets; civilian craft were to register and pass under the earlier agreement, with no seizing of grain under cover of inspection. The third would avoid villages and protect irrigation channels, farmland, and homes.

Any military supplies that had to be requisitioned were to be purchased at stated prices and accompanied by payment vouchers. If a civilian vessel was detained by mistake during an inconclusive inspection, its owner must be compensated for the time lost. Several officers frowned when the censor wrote this into the draft order, fearing merchants would manufacture claims. Fu Jian ordered traders from both banks to choose guarantors as witnesses, with disputed claims subject to another review by army command.

Qin encampments rose outside the city, watchtowers joining one to the next. No assault drums sounded, but every day soldiers measured another footpath. When word first came that the northern army had arrived, panic seized Jiankang. Several great families with grain already stored carried their valuables east of the river overnight. Townspeople hurried to flee, and ox carts clogged the alleys.

After several days, with no battering at the gates and crops still standing in the fields, people dared come out to look. Qin craftsmen replaced a rotten axle in a nearby village’s waterwheel, then returned to camp at night. Several roaming horsemen disturbed an orchard and were marched back by their own patrol officer; compensation was paid the next day according to the regulations.

From the northern wall Liu Yu saw a military line that did not rush upon the city. He ordered the records of goods inspected at the west gate brought up to him. A siege was still a siege even without an assault. Qin allowed civilian food in but rigorously blocked weapons and reinforcements; a city’s defenders could not live forever on rice sold by roadside traders. Yet Liu Yu could not order all grain passing through Qin checkpoints confiscated either. Once rice entered the city, people needed to eat it. If he starved the citizens in order to prevent spies, what would make the Beifu Army any different from another Huan Xuan?

“Let the grain carts in,” he told the gate commander. “Inspect for weapons, trade at market price. If the government granary falls short, borrow from the great families' stores and write down what must be repaid.”

An officer said the great families might refuse to lend. Liu Yu replied that they must first list what each family had already lent; failure to declare stored grain would be examined separately. Every military camp, too, must draw from the same supply ledger. Any commander who requisitioned neighborhood rice by private note would face charges as in the earlier double-levy case at Yongxing Ward.

That evening a party of Beifu light troops tested Qin’s western flank, attempting to burn the grain platforms. Qin sentries failed to notice them at first, and several timber posts were already cut when the alarm bell sounded. Yet the eastern and western camps did not race to the rescue in confusion. The defenders moved their grain by a rear path and caught the raiders between two stockade walls. Jin soldiers withdrew into a bamboo grove. Qin cavalry followed for half a li before their commandant reined them in: beyond the bamboo lay a village, and further pursuit would carry the fighting into people’s homes. The officer clenched his teeth under his men’s reproaches, but still halted at the edge of the grove as ordered.

Seven days later, disaster struck the Qin camp. A unit of guards, short of food after long rain, entered a manor on the southern outskirts without authorization. Claiming they had to inspect private stores because army provisions were almost exhausted, they forced their way into the inner house and seized bronze vessels and silk. The estate steward tried to stop them and was beaten unconscious in the struggle. By daybreak he was dead. Their leader was a collateral kinsman of the Fu clan who had distinguished himself during the rescue at the Fei River. Several comrades pleaded for him, saying he had merely taken the enemy’s property. How could soldiers maintain a siege, they asked, if they lacked food?

The military magistrate investigated the case openly in front of the estate. The private storehouse indeed contained thousands of measures of rice, and local merchants had already intended to sell it to army command. But the three officers had no warrant from the central army; after dividing up the grain they had stolen private possessions as well, and the steward’s death was unrelated to the need to inspect supplies. The royal kinsman protested, pointing at Fu Jian and saying that he had taken an arrow at the Fei River—did his life count for less than a Jin steward’s? Fu Jian made him recite his pay, military land, and injury benefits item by item, then asked which of the bronze dishes or rolls of silk could feed a soldier.
“I take the realm for Your Majesty!” the man shouted. “Am I forbidden to take even a little from the people of that realm?”

Fu Jian did not argue with him in the courtyard. Once the facts were established, the three principal offenders were executed under military law. Others who had taken property were punished according to their roles; everything seized was returned and the dead man’s family received a compensation voucher. Before execution the kinsman still cried out that he was wronged. Some of his comrades wept; others muttered that the Heavenly King cared only for southerners. Fu Jian did not forbid their complaints. He ordered the complete case posted in every camp, omitting neither the merit they had earned at the Fei nor the crimes they had since committed at Jiankang.

By the tenth day two opposing rumors circulated within Jiankang. One held that Qin soldiers truly left civilian houses alone and that villages outside the walls had brought in their autumn harvest. The other claimed that this was merely the emperor’s ruse, and that once the gates opened he would impose Chang’an’s old laws all over again. Several great families sent peace terms through merchants: first they asked whether their estates could be preserved, then what would become of the Jin emperor and his ancestral temple. Townspeople asked more plainly whether a household that had once owned a sack of rice could still buy a few measures, and whether medicines and bandages could reach the wounded men’s camp from traders beyond the walls.

Liu Yu ordered government stores, civilian stores, and the great families' grain-loan vouchers kept in separate accounts. The old Jingkou units were to report their wounded squad by squad. Reading the name of the Wu family east of the city, he remembered the woman who had put straw sandals on her dead son and ordered the compensation overlooked in her case made good. That night someone requested the arrest of those calling for peace. Liu Yu ordered an inquiry only into illicit weapons for the enemy or secret plans to set fires. Mere argument in favor of negotiations was not grounds for imprisonment.

Nor was there peace within the Qin camps. Grain had to cross the Yangtze by boat; illnesses spread through the rain, and fodder for horses was much harder to obtain than in the north. Fu Pi wrote urging an early decision. In Chang’an, Fu Hong supervised shipments and asked how many more ten-day periods each camp could hold out; if they intended to besiege the city through winter, they must first calculate losses in the granaries north of the river. Fu Jian read both letters but issued no decree to storm Jiankang. He summoned Zhu Xu and asked whether he might enter the city to talk.

Zhu Xu had returned south long ago and never wore a Qin official seal when crossing the frontier. This time he came to the new Qin camp with a relief fleet, carrying a register of medicine for refugees from the south. His old crimson Jin official robe had faded almost white from washing. Others expected him to demand immediately that Qin withdraw for the sake of his native state. Instead he first asked whether wounded prisoners could be exchanged and merchant craft allowed to pass on schedule. Only after nightfall did he enter the main tent.
“Liu Yu may not trust me,” Zhu Xu said.
“It’s enough that he hears what you have to say,” Fu Jian replied. “He will know himself whether the people in the city wish to talk.”
Fu Rong listened beside them and slowly adjusted his wooden crutch. “And if he will speak of nothing but withdrawal?”
“Then we must hear that too.”

Zhu Xu looked at Fu Jian. More than twenty years earlier, when Xiangyang fell and he was brought captive into Qin territory, the Heavenly King had promised that he need not forfeit his loyalty to Jin. Only now did those words reveal their full weight. Zhu Xu felt no gratitude for the massed army outside the city, yet neither could he pretend that the people waiting for their wounds to be dressed, to return home, and to bury their dead did not exist. At dawn he took two attendants in a skiff toward Jiankang. They carried no weapons or armor, but at Qin’s second checkpoint they still submitted their transit document for inspection as required.

Archers on the city walls drew their bows. Liu Yu stood behind the battlements and watched Zhu Xu disembark. He first checked that the attendants carried no blades, then ordered a small postern opened to admit him.

Since the day the Beifu Army and Qin forces had faced each other along the Yangtze, the people of Jiankang had waited for the first beat of the assault drums. Now the gate turned slowly on its hinges without a drum sounding. Many within the city leaned out beneath their windows to see what message this aged minister had brought—a man who, under two dynasties, had never lightly allowed anyone else to decide where his allegiance lay.
